title: Event Ticket Booking
prompt: Design a site that sells tickets to concerts and sports events, where people pick exact seats and a big on-sale can draw millions of fans in the first few minutes.

clarify.q: Are seats assigned (pick seat 14 in row F) or general admission (any of 5,000 floor spots)?
clarify.why: Assigned seats make every seat its own row to fight over. General admission is just a counter, which is far easier to make correct and fast.

clarify.q: How long may a fan hold seats while they pay?
clarify.why: The hold length sets how long inventory looks sold but is not. Too long and seats sit idle in abandoned carts. Too short and people lose seats mid-payment.

clarify.q: How big is the largest on-sale, in fans arriving and seats on offer?
clarify.why: A 60,000-seat stadium with 1.5 M fans is a different system from a 300-seat club. The ratio decides whether we need a waiting room at all.

clarify.q: Is there a per-person ticket limit, and do we care about bots and resellers?
clarify.why: Limits and bot defence change identity checks at the queue entrance and add a per-account counter to the purchase transaction.

clarify.q: Do we resell returned or expired seats automatically?
clarify.why: If expired holds go straight back on sale, the seat map must update within seconds and the sweeper becomes part of the critical path.

clarify.q: Which payment methods, and is payment ours or a provider's?
clarify.why: Slow methods (bank redirects, 3-D Secure) can outlast a short hold. That decides whether a hold can be extended once payment starts.

clarify.q: Is a sold ticket ever allowed to be sold twice, even for a minute?
clarify.why: The expected answer is never. That rules out eventually consistent stores as the source of truth for seat state.

functional: Fans browse events and see a seat map with availability no more than a few seconds stale.
A fan can hold up to 8 specific seats for 8 minutes while they pay.
Paying within the hold turns held seats into issued tickets; an expired hold returns the seats to sale.
During a high-demand on-sale, fans wait in a virtual queue and are admitted in a fair order.
Each account is limited to a per-event ticket cap set by the organiser.
nonFunctional: Zero double sales: a seat is issued to at most one order, always.
Hold request p99 under 300 ms for admitted users, even at the peak of an on-sale.
The waiting room absorbs 300,000 requests/s at the edge without touching the booking database.
Browsing stays up (99.95%) even if checkout is degraded; checkout targets 99.9%.
A fan never pays without a ticket: any charge without issued seats is refunded within minutes.
outOfScope: Resale and ticket transfer between fans.
Dynamic pricing algorithms (we store the price; we do not set it).
Physical entry scanning at the gate.

assumptions: 1 M tickets sold per day across all events in normal times
Biggest on-sale: one 60,000-seat stadium show, 1.5 M fans arrive in the first 5 minutes
Average order is 3 seats; a checkout takes about 4 minutes
Without a waiting room, each fan refreshes about every 5 s
A ticket record is about 500 bytes

steps.label: Normal booking rate
steps.math: 1 M tickets / 3 per order = 333 k orders/day; 333 k / 86 400 s ≈ 3.9/s
steps.result: ≈ 4 orders/s, peaks maybe 40/s. Trivial on its own.

steps.label: On-sale traffic with no queue
steps.result: 300 k req/s aimed at one event's seats. This, not the booking rate, is the problem.

steps.label: Orders to sell out
steps.result: Only 20 k fans of 1.5 M can succeed: about 1 in 75.

steps.label: Admitted shoppers and sell-out time
steps.math: Cap 5 000 shoppers at once; 5 000 / 240 s ≈ 21 orders/s; 20 000 / 21 ≈ 960 s
steps.result: ≈ 16 minutes to sell out at 5 k concurrent shoppers

steps.label: Database writes at the peak
steps.math: 21 orders/s × 3 seats ≈ 63 seat updates/s; with ~3 lost races per win, ~190 attempts/s
steps.result: A few hundred small transactions/s: one Postgres primary handles it

steps.label: Ticket storage
steps.result: ≈ 180 GB/year: one database, partitioned by event date

estimates.takeaway: The write volume is tiny; a single relational primary per region can own seat state with real transactions. The danger is a read and retry storm of about 300 k req/s against one event. So the design is two systems: an edge waiting room that turns 1.5 M arrivals into a steady trickle of about 21 orders/s, and a small, strongly consistent booking core behind it. Admit too many and the core thrashes on contention; admit too few and the sale drags on.

api.note: One queue ticket per account per event. Polling the same endpoint with the ticket returns the position, then a signed admission token.
Served from a 1 s cache. The static seat layout comes from the CDN separately.
Idempotency-Key header. All-or-nothing: if one seat is gone, nothing is held.
Idempotency-Key header. Moves the hold to 'paying' and extends it once.
The client polls or listens on a push channel until status is issued or failed.
The fan releases seats early; returns them to sale at once.

entities.name: Seat
entities.why: One row per seat per event. The conditional update on this row is what prevents double booking.

entities.name: Hold
entities.why: The cart. Lets the sweeper and the payment saga find every seat in one place.

entities.name: Order / Ticket
entities.why: The durable result. holdId unique means a retried checkout cannot create two orders.

entities.name: Queue entry
entities.why: Millions of short-lived entries, read and written fast. Losing it is bad but recoverable: fans rejoin.

data.note: Seat state lives in a relational database because the core operation is "change these 3 rows only if all 3 are still free", which is exactly a transaction. Partition seats by eventId so one hot on-sale does not bloat indexes for every other event. The availability endpoint never reads the Seat table directly during a sale: a small job builds a per-section bitmap every second from it and caches it. The queue lives in Redis because it is huge, short-lived and not money.

hld.summary:
Requests hit a CDN and an edge layer first. Static content (event pages, seat layouts) is cached there. During a flagged on-sale the edge also enforces the waiting room: any request to the booking paths without a valid signed admission token is sent to the queue page. A queue service hands out positions and an admitter releases tokens at a rate driven by how many shoppers are active.

Behind the edge, the booking service is stateless and owns all writes to seat state in Postgres. Holds are conditional updates. Checkout starts a small saga: mark the hold as paying, call the payment provider, then issue tickets or release seats and refund. An availability builder turns seat rows into bitmaps every second for the read path, and a sweeper returns expired holds to sale.

diagram.title: Waiting room in front of a small consistent core
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  F[Fans] --> E["CDN and edge token check"]
  E -->|no token| Q[Queue service]
  Q --> R[("Redis queue")]
  A[Admitter] --> R
  A -->|issue signed tokens| Q
  E -->|valid token| B[Booking service]
  B --> DB[("Postgres seats and holds")]
  B --> P[Payment provider]
  AV[Availability builder] --> DB
  AV --> C[("Bitmap cache")]
  E -->|seat map| C
  S[Hold sweeper] --> DB

flows.title: Joining the on-sale
steps: Fan opens the event 10 minutes early and gets a queue ticket; everyone who arrives before the sale opens gets a random position.
The client polls every 10–20 s; the edge answers from the queue service, never from the booking core.
The admitter checks active shoppers (say 4,200 of a 5,000 cap) and issues 800 more admission tokens in queue order.
The token is an HMAC-signed blob with accountId, eventId and a 15-minute expiry; the edge verifies it with no database call.

flows.title: Holding and buying seats
steps: Fan picks 3 seats from the cached bitmap and sends a hold request with an idempotency key.
Booking service runs one transaction: update the 3 seat rows where status is available (or held but expired); if fewer than 3 rows change, roll back and return 409.
Fan submits payment; the hold moves to paying and its expiry extends once to 15 minutes.
Provider confirms; the service marks seats sold and issues tickets in one transaction keyed by holdId.
If confirmation arrives after the seats were lost (should be rare), the saga refunds automatically.

flows.title: An abandoned cart
steps: Fan closes the tab with seats held.
Any later hold request already treats those seats as free once holdExpiresAt passes (lazy expiry).
The sweeper runs every 10 s and flips expired holds to expired, clearing the seat rows so the bitmap shows them available.

deepDives.title: No double booking: how to lock seats
deepDives.problem: Two fans click the same seat within the same millisecond. Exactly one must win, and a fan holding 3 seats must get all 3 or none. At the peak we see a few hundred hold attempts per second, heavily concentrated on the best sections, so contention on single rows is real.

options.name: Pessimistic row locks
options.how: BEGIN; SELECT the seats FOR UPDATE ordered by seatId; check they are free; UPDATE; COMMIT.
pros: Easy to reason about
Works for any rule you can write in SQL
cons: Losers wait on the lock and then fail anyway, holding connections
Must lock in a fixed order or you get deadlocks

options.name: Conditional update (optimistic)
options.how: UPDATE seat SET status='held', holdId=$h, holdExpiresAt=now()+8min WHERE eventId=$e AND seatId = ANY($ids) AND (status='available' OR (status='held' AND holdExpiresAt < now())); commit only if the row count equals the number of seats.
pros: One round trip, short lock time
Losers fail fast with a clear 409
Lazy expiry built into the WHERE clause
cons: Rules must fit a single WHERE clause
Many losers under heavy contention means wasted attempts

options.name: Redis lock per seat, database for the sale
options.how: SET seat:{e}:{s} holdId NX PX 480000 for each seat; on payment, write the sale to the database.
pros: Very fast
TTL expiry is free
cons: Two sources of truth that can disagree after a failover
Multi-seat all-or-nothing needs a Lua script
A lost Redis write can let a seat be held twice

deepDives.choice: Use the conditional update in Postgres. At about 200 attempts/s the database is nowhere near its limit, and keeping seat state in one transactional store means there is no second truth to reconcile. A unique index is not enough on its own here because the seat row already exists; the guard is the status predicate plus the row count. I would move to a per-event in-memory allocator (one owner process per event, writing behind to the database) only if a single event needed thousands of writes per second, which our numbers do not show.

diagram.title: Two fans race for the same seat
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Fan A
  participant B as Fan B
  participant S as Booking service
  participant D as Postgres
  A->>S: hold seats 14 15 16
  B->>S: hold seats 15 16 17
  S->>D: conditional update for A
  D-->>S: 3 rows updated
  S-->>A: 201 hold until 20:08
  S->>D: conditional update for B
  D-->>S: 1 row updated, roll back
  S-->>B: 409 seats 15 and 16 taken

deepDives.title: Holds with a time limit
deepDives.problem: A hold must expire on its own when a fan walks away, but must not expire while their payment is in flight. If the hold lapses after the card is charged, we have taken money for seats someone else might now own.

options.name: Lazy expiry plus a sweeper
options.how: Store holdExpiresAt on the seat. The hold query treats expired holds as free. A sweeper every 10 s cleans up so the bitmap is accurate.
pros: Correctness does not depend on the sweeper running on time
No extra infrastructure
cons: Seat map shows an expired seat as held until the next sweep
Sweeper must be idempotent and batched

options.name: Delayed message per hold
options.how: Publish a 'release at T' message to a delay queue when the hold is created.
pros: Expiry is pushed exactly on time
cons: Correctness depends on the queue firing; a stuck queue leaves seats locked
Cancelling messages on purchase is fiddly

options.name: Two-phase hold: browsing then paying
options.how: On checkout, flip the hold to 'paying' with one extension to 15 minutes. Only the payment saga can move it out of paying.
pros: Removes the charge-after-expiry race for normal cases
Clear state for support staff
cons: A crashed saga can keep seats locked until a hard cap
Fans can game it by starting slow payments

deepDives.choice: Combine lazy expiry with the paying state. Lazy expiry means correctness never depends on a background job. The paying state stops the common race. For the rare case where the provider confirms after a hard 15-minute cap, the saga's compensation step refunds and tells the fan. If the business wanted longer holds (say, 20 minutes for group bookings) I would add a visible countdown and an "I'm still here" extension rather than a longer default, because every minute of hold is a minute a seat sits unsold during a sale.

deepDives.title: The virtual waiting room
deepDives.problem: 1.5 M fans arrive for 20,000 successful orders. If they all reach the booking service, the database burns its capacity on failed contention and the site falls over for everyone, including people buying tickets to other events.

options.name: Rate limit only
options.how: Return 429 above N requests/s per event.
pros: Trivial to add
cons: Rewards whoever retries fastest, which means bots
Fans get errors with no idea how long to wait

options.name: Queue with signed admission tokens
options.how: Edge sends unadmitted traffic to a queue page. An admitter issues tokens in queue order at a rate that keeps active shoppers under a cap. The edge checks the token signature locally.
pros: Booking core sees a steady, sized load
Fans see a position and an ETA
Token check costs no database call
cons: Another system to run and test before every big sale
Token sharing must be blocked by binding it to account and device

options.name: Lottery before the sale
options.how: Fans register in advance; winners get a purchase window.
pros: Fairest against bots
Demand known in advance
cons: Bad user experience for walk-up buyers
Needs organiser buy-in and a different product flow

deepDives.choice: Build the queue with signed tokens, turned on per event when expected demand exceeds about 5× seats. The admitter is a feedback loop: it reads active shoppers and the hold error rate every few seconds and admits more only while both are healthy, so a slow payment provider automatically slows admission. For the very largest shows (demand above 50× seats) I would offer the organiser the lottery mode, because no queue makes a 1-in-75 chance feel fair.

deepDives.title: Fairness and bots
deepDives.problem: Fair has two parts: arrival order is respected, and one person does not take a hundred places. Bots can open thousands of sessions and refresh faster than any human.

options.name: Strict first come, first served
options.how: Queue position is the arrival timestamp.
pros: Easy to explain
cons: Before the sale opens, being first is about refreshing at exactly 10:00:00, which favours bots and low latency
Clock skew across edge nodes matters

options.name: Random order for the pre-sale crowd, then arrival order
options.how: Anyone in the queue before the start time gets a random position; later arrivals queue behind in arrival order.
pros: Removes the incentive to hammer at the opening second
Still rewards showing up early
cons: Fans may feel a late friend got lucky
Needs clear messaging

deepDives.choice: Use random order for early arrivals and arrival order after the start. Combine it with one queue entry per verified account (phone or prior purchase), a challenge at queue entry rather than at checkout, and the per-account cap enforced inside the hold transaction (count of held plus sold seats for this account and event). If bot traffic still dominated, I would add the lottery mode rather than harder captchas, which mostly punish humans.

failures: Payment provider slows to 10 s per call during the on-sale
The admitter sees fewer completed checkouts and admits fewer fans; holds in paying state are protected by the extension; the queue ETA rises instead of errors.
Synchronous replica promotes in under 30 s; holds are idempotent by key so retries are safe; the admitter pauses admission until hold latency recovers.
Replicas take over; if positions are lost, fans keep their queue ticket in a signed cookie that carries their original position, so they can rejoin in place.
No double booking because lazy expiry is in the hold query; the seat map just shows some stale held seats; alert when the oldest expired hold is more than 60 s past its time.
Fan is charged but the ticket issue step fails
The saga retries issuing by holdId; after a fixed number of retries it refunds and alerts; a nightly job compares provider charges with issued orders.
Availability cache serves a 30 s old bitmap
Fans pick seats that are gone and get 409s; return the fresh status of those seats in the 409 and suggest the nearest free block.
scale: 10× events, same peak size: nothing changes in the core; partition by eventId already spreads load; more booking service pods.
A 100 k-seat event with 10 M fans: the queue grows to about 1 GB in Redis and the edge carries the load; admission cap stays tied to what the core can do, so the sale simply takes longer.
Thousands of hold writes/s on one event: move that event's seats to a single-owner in-memory allocator with a write-ahead log, and keep Postgres as the record of sold tickets.
Global sales: one booking region per event (pinned by venue), with the queue and edge served globally; never split one event's seats across regions.

followups.q: How would you handle general admission instead of seats?
answer: Keep a counter row per price zone: UPDATE zone SET held = held + n WHERE held + sold + n <= capacity.
A single hot row caps throughput, so split it into 10–20 sub-counters and pick one at random, borrowing from siblings when one runs dry.
Holds and expiry work the same way, keyed by hold instead of seat.

followups.q: Can the seat map be real-time instead of a 1 s cache?
answer: Push changed-seat deltas over a websocket from the availability builder.
It is still stale by network delay, so the hold transaction stays the only truth.
Real-time costs fan-out to 5,000 shoppers per change; batch deltas every 500 ms to keep it cheap.

followups.q: What if a fan opens two tabs and holds seats in both?
answer: The per-account cap counts held plus sold seats across all holds for the event.
Optionally allow one active hold per account and make a new hold release the old one.
Both checks happen inside the same transaction as the seat update.

followups.q: How do you test the on-sale before the real one?
answer: Replay a recorded traffic shape against a staging event with synthetic accounts.
Run a game day where the payment provider is slowed on purpose to check the admitter backs off.
Pre-scale the edge and the booking pods 30 minutes before the start; do not rely on autoscaling reacting in time.

followups.q: Where does the saga live and what if it crashes?
answer: The checkout state is in the Hold and Order rows, not in memory, so any worker can resume it.
A recovery job picks up holds stuck in paying for over 2 minutes and asks the provider for the payment status by our idempotency key.
Every step is keyed by holdId, so running it twice changes nothing.

mistakes: Spending the time on database sharding when the numbers show about 200 writes/s; the real problem is 300 k read and retry requests/s.
Using a cache or Redis TTL as the only record of who holds a seat.
Letting hold expiry depend on a background job firing on time.
Rate limiting with 429s and calling it a waiting room; that rewards bots that retry fastest.
Forgetting the case where payment succeeds after the hold has expired.

mid: Asked whether seats are assigned or general admission before designing
Stated a hold time and what happens when it runs out
Used a database transaction or conditional update so one seat cannot be sold twice
Made hold and checkout requests idempotent with a key
Drew separate read (seat map) and write (hold) paths
senior: Showed with numbers that the on-sale is a read and retry storm, not a write-throughput problem
Compared at least two locking approaches and justified the choice from the contention level
Used lazy expiry so correctness does not depend on the sweeper
Handled payment success after hold expiry with a compensating refund
Designed the waiting room with signed tokens checked at the edge and an admission rate tied to backend health
staff: Defined fairness explicitly (random order for early arrivals, one entry per account) and its trade-offs
Isolated on-sale load so other events and browsing keep working
Described how the sale is rehearsed and pre-scaled rather than trusting autoscaling
Named the threshold at which they would move one event to a single-owner in-memory allocator
